new.title: Order the quenelle at Café Comptoir Abel
new.desc: Opened in 1928 inside a far older inn near Ainay, Abel is often called the oldest bouchon still serving in Lyon. Creaking wood, small rooms and the pike quenelle baked in its sauce are the reasons people keep coming back.
new.tip: Book, especially at the weekend, and come hungry: the quenelle alone is a meal. It carries the official Bouchons Lyonnais label.
new.q: Café Comptoir Abel, 25 Rue Guynemer, Lyon

new.title: Join the Friday frog night at Café Lobut in Villeurbanne
new.desc: A Formica-counter neighbourhood bouchon on Cours Tolstoï that has fed Villeurbanne since 1949. In 2025 the guardians of the authentic bouchon tradition named it the best in the Lyon area, a surprise win for a spot far from the tourist trail.
new.tip: Friday evenings are for frogs' legs and Saturday mornings for a mâchon of charcuterie and wine. Reserve, the locals do.
new.q: Café Lobut, 50 Cours Tolstoï, Villeurbanne

new.title: Dine at the Bouchon des Filles on the Croix-Rousse slopes
new.desc: Opened in 2007 by a team of women, this bouchon on Rue Sergent Blandan gives the old canteen of the silk workers a warm, relaxed twist. The set menu keeps prices gentle and the Lyonnais classics generous.
new.tip: It serves dinner every evening, which makes it a good bet on a Sunday or Monday when many bouchons are shut.
new.q: Le Bouchon des Filles, 20 Rue Sergent Blandan, Lyon

new.title: Try poulet au vinaigre at Chez Hugon
new.desc: A tiny, red-checked bouchon behind the Hôtel de Ville with a long line of women at the stove. Regulars swear by the chicken in vinegar sauce, the andouillette with mustard and a glass of Beaujolais or a Picon bière.
new.tip: It is closed at weekends and usually in August, and the room is small, so book for a weekday.
new.q: Chez Hugon, 12 Rue Pizay, Lyon

new.title: Splurge at La Mère Brazier, where the mères made history
new.desc: Eugénie Brazier's restaurant on Rue Royale made her the first chef to hold three Michelin stars at two restaurants at once, in 1933. Chef Mathieu Viannay revived the house in 2008 and still serves her Bresse chicken in the original tiled rooms.
new.tip: Lunch menus are the gentlest way in. Book well ahead for a weekend.
new.q: La Mère Brazier, 12 Rue Royale, Lyon

new.title: Take a coffee under the mirrors of the Grand Café des Négociants
new.desc: Since 1864 merchants, bankers and shoppers have met in this Second Empire café by the Cordeliers, all chandeliers, gilt and walls of mirrors. It is one of the grand old rooms of the Presqu'île and serves from morning to late evening.
new.tip: Sit inside rather than on the terrace to get the full décor. It is a handy stop between Rue de la République and the Rhône.
new.q: Grand Café des Négociants, 1 Place Francisque Régaud, Lyon

new.title: Taste a Palet d'Or at Bernachon
new.desc: The Bernachon family has made chocolate on Cours Franklin Roosevelt for generations. Its Palet d'Or, a disc of ganache made with Isigny cream and topped with gold leaf, has followed the same recipe since the 1970s.
new.tip: The tea room next to the shop is a fine place for a slice of cake. Expect queues before Christmas and Easter.
new.q: Bernachon, 42 Cours Franklin Roosevelt, Lyon

new.title: Pick a pastry at Bouillet on Place de la Croix-Rousse
new.desc: Sébastien Bouillet took over his father's Croix-Rousse pastry shop in 2000 and turned it into one of Lyon's best-known names in cakes and chocolate. The original shop still sits on the plateau's main square.
new.tip: Next door at number 16, his retro shop Goûter sells old-fashioned cakes for an afternoon snack. Combine it with the morning market on the boulevard.
new.q: Bouillet, 15 Place de la Croix-Rousse, Lyon

new.title: Graze the street food containers at HEAT
new.desc: In a former boilermaking workshop at Confluence, HEAT is a half-open food hall built around four shipping containers whose cooks change every week. DJ sets, talks and workshops keep the place busy beyond mealtimes.
new.tip: Check the line-up on its website before you go, then walk down Quai Perrache towards the Musée des Confluences.
new.q: HEAT, 70 Quai Perrache, Lyon

new.title: Shop the riverside market on Quai Victor Augagneur
new.desc: Along the Rhône on the left bank, around fifty traders set up on Friday, Saturday and Sunday mornings with fruit, cheese, meat, fish, roast chickens, wine and flowers. A smaller session runs on Thursday afternoon for after-work shopping.
new.tip: Come early on Sunday, then take your picnic down the steps to the riverbank lawns.
new.q: Marché Quai Victor Augagneur, Lyon

new.title: Order an old fashioned at L'Antiquaire
new.desc: A dim, speakeasy-style cocktail bar near the Terreaux, with brick walls, antique bric-a-brac, Chesterfield banquettes and jazz in the background. The old fashioned is the drink it is known for.
new.tip: It fills up fast at weekends; arrive early in the evening.
new.q: L'Antiquaire, 20 Rue Hippolyte Flandrin, Lyon

new.title: Dine amid Art Nouveau tiles at the Brasserie des Brotteaux
new.desc: Built in 1913 as an Eden-Bar beside the old Brotteaux station, this corner brasserie keeps its ceramics by Louis Muller, its ironwork and chandeliers. The Blanc-Brude family gave it its current name in 1948.
new.tip: Ask for a table in the main room to see the tiles. Afterwards look at the old station building on Place Jules Ferry.
new.q: Brasserie des Brotteaux, 1 Place Jules Ferry, Lyon

new.title: Eat bistro style at L'Art et la Manière in Guillotière
new.desc: For more than twenty years this bistro on Grande Rue de la Guillotière has been a neighbourhood favourite, with seasonal market cooking and a well-chosen wine list in a relaxed room.
new.tip: Combine it with a wander around the mixed streets of Guillotière and the Rhône banks just west.
new.q: L'Art et la Manière, 102 Grande Rue de la Guillotière, Lyon

new.title: Eat quenelles where Guignol once played, at the Café du Soleil
new.desc: On Place de la Trinité in Saint-Georges, the Café du Soleil claims roots in the 18th century and is said to be the oldest restaurant in Lyon. Its facade was the traditional backdrop for Guignol, and its quenelles have been made by hand on site since 2005.
new.tip: Look up at the sun on the corner of the building before going in. The square is the start of the Montée du Gourguillon.
new.q: Café du Soleil, 2 Rue Saint-Georges, Lyon

new.title: Settle onto the worn benches of Bouchon Léa
new.desc: Serving Lyonnais classics since 1943, Léa sits on a small square by the Saône and keeps its wood panelling and well-worn benches. It carries the Bouchons Lyonnais quality label.
new.tip: Good after a Sunday morning at the Saint-Antoine market or the Marché de la Création across the river.
new.q: Bouchon Léa, 11 Place Antonin Gourju, Lyon

new.title: Meet Lyon's past and its puppets at Gadagne
new.desc: The Renaissance Hôtel de Gadagne in Vieux Lyon holds two museums: the history of Lyon and the arts of the puppet, from Guignol to puppets from around the world. It also has a small theatre and a hanging garden above the rooftops.
new.tip: Climb to the garden café at the top for a quiet drink with a view of Fourvière.
new.q: Gadagne, 1 Place du Petit Collège, Lyon

new.title: Learn about the Resistance at the CHRD
new.desc: Lyon was called the capital of the French Resistance, and this centre tells that story in the former military health school that the Gestapo used under Klaus Barbie. Testimonies, documents and temporary exhibitions cover resistance and deportation.
new.tip: Allow two hours. It opens Wednesday to Sunday; tram T2 stops at Centre Berthelot right outside.
new.q: Centre d'Histoire de la Résistance et de la Déportation, 14 Avenue Berthelot, Lyon

new.title: See the glass vault Jean Nouvel put on the Opéra
new.desc: Behind the 1831 facades of the old Grand Théâtre, Jean Nouvel built an entirely new opera house between 1989 and 1993, digging five floors underground and crowning it with a glass vault. A ballet studio sits right under the roof.
new.tip: Look under the arcades in the evening: breakdancers have practised here since the 1990s.
new.q: Opéra de Lyon, Place de la Comédie, Lyon

new.title: Step into Saint-Nizier, the church of the Presqu'île
new.desc: Saint-Nizier stands in the heart of the Presqu'île and has long rivalled the cathedral in prestige. In June 1975 it made headlines when sex workers occupied it to protest police harassment, a founding moment of their rights movement.
new.tip: It is a few steps from the Cordeliers metro; slip in on your way between the Terreaux and the Jacobins.
new.q: Église Saint-Nizier, Place Saint-Nizier, Lyon

new.title: Find Romanesque calm at the Basilique d'Ainay
new.desc: Hidden among the streets of the elegant Ainay district, this former abbey church is a rare Romanesque building in Lyon, dating from the 12th century. Hippolyte Flandrin painted the golden apse in 1855.
new.tip: Walk round the outside to see the carved stones and the bell tower, then continue to Place Ampère.
new.q: Basilique Saint-Martin d'Ainay, Lyon

new.title: Read the spines on the Bibliothèque de la Cité mural
new.desc: On the corner of Rue de la Platière and the Saône quay, the CitéCréation artists painted a 400 square metre bookcase in 1998, filled with works by more than 300 writers from Lyon and the region. Look for lines by Louise Labé and Frédéric Dard.
new.tip: It faces the Saône, so morning light is best. The Fresque des Lyonnais is a short walk north along the quay.
new.q: Fresque La Bibliothèque de la Cité, Quai de la Pêcherie, Lyon

new.title: Count the 24 columns of the old Palais de Justice
new.desc: Its long row of columns along the Saône earned it the nickname 'the twenty-four columns'. The neoclassical courthouse in Vieux Lyon still hosts the Rhône assize court, and its interior décor is a listed historic monument.
new.tip: See it best from the Passerelle du Palais de Justice footbridge across the river, especially when lit at night.
new.q: Palais de justice historique de Lyon, Quai Romain Rolland, Lyon

new.title: Wander among the tombs of the Cimetière de Loyasse
new.desc: Opened in 1807 on Fourvière hill, Loyasse is Lyon's oldest cemetery still in use, a quiet maze of chapels, sculpted tombs and old trees where the city's great families lie.
new.tip: Walk there from the basilica through the Parc des Hauteurs and over the Passerelle des Quatre-Vents footbridge.
new.q: Cimetière de Loyasse, Lyon

new.title: Find Philibert Delorme's gallery at Hôtel Bullioud
new.desc: In a courtyard on Rue Juiverie, Philibert Delorme built an arched gallery after his journey to Italy in 1536. Its décor is one of the very first experiments with the Renaissance style in France, by the future architect of the Tuileries.
new.tip: Push the door at number 8 when it is open and look up. Rue Juiverie has several other fine Renaissance facades.
new.q: Hôtel Bullioud, 8 Rue Juiverie, Lyon

new.title: Discover Lyon painted by Jean Couty
new.desc: Facing Île Barbe in Saint-Rambert, the house and studio of painter Jean Couty became a museum in 2017. His colourful views of Lyon's churches, rooftops and rivers are shown alongside changing exhibitions.
new.tip: Guided visits run on the first Friday of the month. Cross to Île Barbe afterwards for a riverside stroll.
new.q: Musée Jean Couty, 1 Place Henri Barbusse, Lyon

new.title: Catch a contemporary show at the IAC in Villeurbanne
new.desc: The Institut d'art contemporain is one of France's leading contemporary art centres, tucked into a quiet street of Villeurbanne. It stages bold solo exhibitions and, in Biennale years, a show of young international artists.
new.tip: It opens Wednesday to Friday afternoons, so plan around that. The Gratte-Ciel are a short walk east.
new.q: Institut d'art contemporain, 11 Rue Docteur Dolard, Villeurbanne

new.title: Admire the old exchange on Place du Change
new.desc: The Loge du Change was built between 1631 and 1653 for the merchants and bankers of Lyon's great fairs, and Soufflot, architect of the Paris Panthéon, reworked it around 1750. Since 1803 it has been a Protestant church.
new.tip: Sit on the square at dusk when the facade glows; services are on Sunday morning.
new.q: Temple du Change, Place du Change, Lyon

new.title: Visit the Grande Mosquée de Lyon
new.desc: After years of disputes over its site, Lyon's great mosque on Boulevard Pinel opened in 1994 to designs by architect Robert Ballandras. It can welcome 3,500 worshippers and has a library and a school.
new.tip: Respect prayer times and dress modestly; the European Heritage Days in September are a good moment for a visit.
new.q: Grande Mosquée de Lyon, 146 Boulevard Pinel, Lyon

new.title: Light a candle in Saint-Bonaventure
new.desc: The church of the old Franciscan friary is the only medieval building left in the north of the 2nd arrondissement after Rue de la République was carved through in the 19th century. Pope Francis raised it to a basilica in 2019.
new.tip: It stands on Place des Cordeliers, right by the metro, and is a calm break from shopping.
new.q: Basilique Saint-Bonaventure, Place des Cordeliers, Lyon

new.title: Stroll the glass-roofed Passage de l'Argue
new.desc: Rebuilt in 1828 by Vincent Farge, this 145 metre covered arcade links Rue de la République to Rue de Brest with neoclassical porches, a rotunda and a glass roof hung with lanterns. Matching wooden shopfronts line the whole way.
new.tip: Look for the mirrored heart in the rotunda, which replaced a stolen statue of Mercury.
new.q: Passage de l'Argue, Lyon

new.title: Sit by the Fontaine des Jacobins
new.desc: The fountain at the heart of Place des Jacobins was designed by Gaspard André and inaugurated in 1885. Its four statues honour artists of Lyon: Philibert Delorme, Guillaume Coustou, Gérard Audran and Hippolyte Flandrin.
new.tip: Take a coffee on the square and try to match each statue to its name; Rue Mercière's restaurants start just behind.
new.q: Fontaine des Jacobins, Place des Jacobins, Lyon

new.title: Browse the Sunday Marché de la Création
new.desc: Every Sunday morning since 1979, more than 150 painters, sculptors and other artists line Quai Romain Rolland in Vieux Lyon to sell original works. A committee selects the exhibitors each month, so the line-up keeps changing.
new.tip: Go before noon, then cross the footbridge to the Saint-Antoine food market on the opposite bank.
new.q: Marché de la Création, Quai Romain Rolland, Lyon

new.title: Swim outdoors by the river at the Piscine du Rhône
new.desc: The Centre nautique Tony Bertrand, still called the Piscine du Rhône by locals, sits on the left bank with a 50 metre outdoor pool and, in summer, a huge leisure pool with a paddling area. Swimming lengths beside the Rhône is a Lyon summer ritual.
new.tip: The summer season runs from early June to the end of August; weekday mornings are the least crowded.
new.q: Centre nautique Tony Bertrand, 8 Quai Claude Bernard, Lyon

new.title: Climb the Roman Montée du Gourguillon
new.desc: This steep cobbled lane from Saint-Georges to Saint-Just follows a Roman road that linked the upper town to the river quarters. Old houses and glimpses over the roofs reward the climb.
new.tip: Start at Place de la Trinité, the traditional Guignol backdrop, and keep going up to the Saint-Just funicular station.
new.q: Montée du Gourguillon, Lyon

new.title: Spread a blanket in the Parc de Gerland
new.desc: Built on former industrial land by the Rhône in the south of the city, the 18 hectare Parc de Gerland, renamed Parc Henry-Chabert, is given over to sport and leisure with wide lawns and garden areas.
new.tip: Metro B to Stade de Gerland. Locals cycle here along the Rhône from the centre.
new.q: Parc de Gerland, Lyon

new.title: Go wild by the Rhône in the Parc de la Feyssine
new.desc: At the northern edge of Villeurbanne, this 55 hectare natural urban park runs along the Rhône with meadows, woods and riverside paths. It feels far from the city yet is a tram ride away.
new.tip: Tram T1 towards La Doua. Bring a picnic and follow the paths down to the river.
new.q: Parc de la Feyssine, Villeurbanne

new.title: See something new at Les Subsistances
new.desc: A former military supply depot on the Saône quay has become Les Subs, a creative laboratory for dance, circus, theatre and music where artists come in residence. Its courtyards and esplanade host shows and parties.
new.tip: Check the programme for festivals and free events; the riverside setting is lovely on a summer evening.
new.q: Les Subsistances, 8 bis Quai Saint-Vincent, Lyon

new.title: Catch a play at the Théâtre National Populaire
new.desc: Founded in Paris in 1920 to bring great theatre to everyone, the TNP moved in 1972 to the Gratte-Ciel district of Villeurbanne. It is a national drama centre that creates its own productions and builds its sets on site.
new.tip: Metro A to Gratte-Ciel. Affordable tickets are part of its mission, so look out for low-price deals.
new.q: Théâtre National Populaire, Place Lazare Goujon, Villeurbanne

new.title: Watch an art-house film at Le Zola
new.desc: Villeurbanne's single-screen cinema has shown films on Cours Émile Zola for about a century. Its festivals of Iberian and Latin American cinema, short films and British films are local fixtures.
new.tip: In summer it runs repertory classics; check the programme for original-language screenings.
new.q: Cinéma Le Zola, 117 Cours Émile Zola, Villeurbanne

new.title: Meet crime writers at Quais du Polar
new.desc: Each spring, usually in early April, Lyon hosts one of Europe's biggest crime fiction festivals, with authors from around the world, talks and a huge bookshop in the Palais de la Bourse. Talks and meetings are free.
new.tip: Arrive early for the big-name talks, as seats are first come, first served.
new.q: Palais de la Bourse, Lyon

new.title: Watch silk being printed at the Atelier de Soierie
new.desc: On the Croix-Rousse slopes, this workshop still prints silk by hand with frames, laying down one colour at a time. You can watch the printers at work for free and see the scarves take shape.
new.tip: Visits are free during opening hours; a paid workshop lets you print your own square if you book ahead.
new.q: Atelier de Soierie, 33 Rue Romarin, Lyon

new.title: See a concert in the Halle Tony Garnier
new.desc: Tony Garnier built this vast hall in 1928 as the cattle market of the La Mouche slaughterhouses. Saved and listed in 1975, it became a concert hall in 1988 and is one of the largest in France.
new.tip: Tram T1 stops at Halle Tony Garnier. Look up at the huge roof span as you walk in.
new.q: Halle Tony Garnier, Lyon

new.title: Hunt for treasures at the Puces du Canal
new.desc: Opened in 1995 beside the canal in Villeurbanne, this is the second-largest flea market in France by area, with some 200 permanent dealers and hundreds of outdoor pitches of furniture, vintage and bric-a-brac.
new.tip: It runs on Thursday, Saturday and Sunday mornings; Sunday is the busiest, and the best finds go early.
new.q: Puces du Canal, 3 Rue Eugène Pottier, Villeurbanne
